description: Width tiers for Mathematics Year 8 — ACARA v9
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. Every student in the class reaches this floor.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, contexts or applications — not harder versions of the same context. 2–4 discrete directions per descriptor.

AC9M8N01.minimum_width: Recognise that √2 and π are irrational; explain what makes a number irrational and locate it approximately on the real number line.
AC9M8N01.typical_width: Distinguish rational from irrational numbers across a range of examples including square roots and π; use digital tools to explore decimal expansions; describe the real number system as including both rational and irrational numbers.
wider: Investigate historical approximations to π across multiple cultures — Egyptian, Babylonian, Chinese, Indian, Greek — and evaluate the accuracy achieved by each.
Explore the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 in art and design — verify it is irrational and locate it on the real number line.
Investigate the connection between irrational numbers and Pythagoras' theorem — explore which hypotenuse lengths are irrational.
elaborations: recognising that the real number system includes irrational numbers which can be approximately located on the real number line
using digital tools to systematically explore contexts or situations that use irrational numbers, such as finding the length of the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle
investigating the golden ratio in art and design, and historical approximations to π in different societies
connecting the ratio between the circumference and diameter of any circle to the irrational value of π using circular objects and string or dynamic geometry software

AC9M8N02.minimum_width: Derive and state the product of powers rule from expanded form; apply the product and quotient rules to simplify expressions with the same base.
AC9M8N02.typical_width: Establish all three exponent laws and the zero exponent from expanded form; apply individually and in combination to simplify numerical expressions; verify using digital tools.
wider: Investigate why a⁰ = 1 using the quotient rule pattern — connect to the sequence of decreasing exponents.
Extend the pattern to negative exponents: what would a⁻¹ mean, following the sequence?
Apply exponent laws to scientific notation contexts: multiply and divide numbers expressed as powers of 10.
elaborations: recognising the connection between exponent form and expanded form with the exponent laws of product of powers rule, quotient of powers rule, and power of a power rule
applying the exponent laws individually and in combination to simplify expressions
using digital tools to systematically explore the application of the exponent laws; observing that the bases need to be the same
using examples such as 3⁴/3⁴ = 1 and 3⁴⁻⁴ = 3⁰ to illustrate that for any non-zero natural number a, a⁰ = 1

AC9M8N03.minimum_width: Classify fractions as terminating or recurring by division; write recurring decimals using correct notation.
AC9M8N03.typical_width: Identify terminating, recurring and non-terminating (irrational) decimals; predict whether a fraction terminates from the prime factorisation of its denominator; use digital tools to verify.
wider: Investigate the length of the repeating cycle for unit fractions (1/7, 1/11, 1/13) and look for patterns connecting cycle length to divisibility.
Explore why only factors of 2 and 5 produce terminating decimals in base 10 — connect to the structure of our numeration system.
Investigate 0.999... = 1 using the recurring decimal as an algebraic argument.
elaborations: identifying when a fraction has a terminating decimal expansion from the prime factorisation of its denominator
identifying terminating, recurring and non-terminating decimals and choosing their appropriate representations

AC9M8N04.minimum_width: Apply sign rules for multiplication and division of integers including negative × negative; calculate results involving mixed negative rational numbers.
AC9M8N04.typical_width: Establish sign rules from patterns; apply all four operations to integers and rational numbers including negative fractions; use commutative, associative and distributive properties to select efficient strategies.
wider: Investigate why negative × negative = positive using a number line or debt/removal model as a conceptual justification.
Explore the pattern (−1)ⁿ for increasing n — connect to sign rules and predict for any integer exponent.
Apply efficient strategies to multi-step financial calculations involving positive and negative rational quantities.
elaborations: using patterns to assist in establishing the rules for the multiplication and division of integers
applying and explaining efficient strategies such as using the commutative or associative property for regrouping, partitioning, place value, patterning
recognising the effect of sign in the multiplication of integers; for example, (−1)⁴ = 1 and (−1)⁵ = −1

AC9M8N05.minimum_width: Model a percentage increase or decrease problem; formulate and solve a simple financial problem; interpret the solution in context.
AC9M8N05.typical_width: Apply modelling to percentage increase/decrease (mark-ups, discounts, GST), personal income tax, and environmental/weather contexts with positive and negative quantities; review model appropriateness; communicate solutions.
wider: Investigate successive percentage changes — why does a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease not return to the original? Develop a general model.
Model personal income tax across multiple brackets — calculate effective rate vs marginal rate.
Model environmental contexts involving percentage change over extended periods — connect informally to exponential growth.
elaborations: modelling situations involving weather and environmental contexts including temperature or sea depths by applying operations to positive and negative rational numbers
modelling situations that involve percentage increases or decreases and explaining why it is an increase or decrease, such as mark-ups, discounts, GST
modelling situations involving personal income tax, interpreting tax tables to determine income tax at various levels of income
modelling situations involving percentage increase or decrease such as market trends, effects on population, or effects on the environment over extended periods

AC9M8A01.minimum_width: Expand and simplify a linear expression with one set of brackets; factorise a linear expression by identifying the HCF.
AC9M8A01.typical_width: Create, expand, factorise, rearrange and simplify linear expressions with multiple terms and negative coefficients; apply distributive, associative, commutative, identity and inverse properties explicitly; use algebra tiles or area models to verify.
wider: Investigate the distributive property across subtraction — verify a(b − c) = ab − ac using substitution and area models.
Apply rearrangement to real formulas from science and everyday contexts: rearrange distance = speed × time for speed; area formulas for dimensions.
Explore common expansion errors (e.g. 3(x + 2) = 3x + 2) — explain why the error occurs and construct counterexamples.
elaborations: rearranging and simplifying linear expressions involving variables with integer coefficients and constants; using manipulatives such as algebra tiles
demonstrating the relationship between factorising and expanding linear expressions using manipulatives, such as algebra tiles or area models
using the distributive, associative, commutative, identity and inverse properties to expand and factorise algebraic expressions using strategies such as the area model

AC9M8A02.minimum_width: Graph a linear relation y = mx + b from a table of values; solve a two-step linear equation with unknowns on both sides; verify by substitution.
AC9M8A02.typical_width: Graph linear relations and inequalities on the Cartesian plane; solve linear equations requiring expansion; solve one-variable inequalities including sign reversal; represent solutions on a number line; verify graphically and algebraically.
wider: Solve linear equations arising from geometry problems — find x given angle relationships or perimeter conditions.
Investigate equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions — represent graphically and explain what this means.
Explore compound inequalities (a < x < b) and represent solution sets on a number line.
elaborations: recognising that in a table of values, if the first difference between consecutive values of the dependent variable is constant, then it is a linear relationship
graphing linear functions and relations including inequalities
completing a table of values, plotting the resulting points on the Cartesian plane and determining whether the relationship is linear
solving linear equations of the form ax + b = c and one-variable inequalities
solving linear equations such as 3x + 7 = 6x − 9, representing these graphically, and verifying solutions by substitution

AC9M8A03.minimum_width: Formulate a linear function for a practical context with a constant rate and fixed component; use it to answer a specific question; identify one limitation of the model.
AC9M8A03.typical_width: Formulate and solve linear models for varied applied contexts (taxi fares, pay rates, motion); choose appropriate representation (table, graph, equation); interpret solutions; review model appropriateness including domain and linearity assumptions.
wider: Compare two linear models on the same axes (e.g. two taxi companies) — find the break-even point algebraically and interpret in context.
Model patterns on Country/Place with linear functions — investigate Indigenous knowledge connections and use the model as a predictive tool.
Apply linear modelling to financial contexts comparing different pay structures (base + commission vs flat rate) — model, compare and advise.
elaborations: modelling situations involving linear functions, including practical contexts such as taxi fares involving flag fall fees, motion in a straight line
modelling problems in practical situations and interpreting solutions within the context of the problem, including giving attention to all units of measurement
modelling financial problems involving pay rates, using a table of values to represent the pay amounts and hours worked using an hourly rate of pay
modelling patterns on Country/Place and exploring their connections and meaning to linear equations, using the model as a predictive tool

AC9M8A04.minimum_width: Using graphing software, vary m in y = mx + b across positive, negative and zero values; describe the effect on the graph and state a general rule.
AC9M8A04.typical_width: Systematically vary both m and b using digital tools; make and test conjectures about parallel lines, gradient, and intercept; generalise the effect of each parameter; investigate integer solutions to two-variable equations.
wider: Investigate what value of m produces a line perpendicular to a given line — discover the relationship m₁ × m₂ = −1 informally.
Explore how linear functions are used in linear regression models in machine learning — describe what the gradient and intercept represent in this context.
Investigate integer solutions to 2x + 3y = 48 — use digital tools to find all solutions and represent on the Cartesian plane.
elaborations: using graphing software to investigate the effect of systematically varying parameters of linear functions on the corresponding graphs, making and testing conjectures
using graphing software to systematically contrast the graphs of y = 2x, y = −2x, y = 2x and y = −2x
using digital tools to investigate integer solutions to equations such as 2x + 3y = 48
exploring how linear functions are used in linear regression models as a statistical technique in machine learning

AC9M8M01.minimum_width: Decompose a composite shape into two known shapes and calculate the total area; estimate the area of an irregular shape using a grid overlay.
AC9M8M01.typical_width: Determine area and perimeter of composite shapes by composing or decomposing; apply to shapes requiring subtracted regions; use increasingly accurate measurement approximations for irregular shapes.
wider: Apply area estimation to real-world irregular shapes: estimate the area of a land parcel or ecological survey region from a map or aerial image.
Investigate floor plan problems requiring area calculation for irregular rooms — apply to real building design contexts.
Explore how numerical integration methods formalise grid-based area estimation — informal preview of calculus concepts.
elaborations: determining the area of composite shapes by composing or decomposing shapes
using arrays and rectangles to approximate the area of irregular shapes in situations such as a council needing to work out how much mosquito spray to use
determining the perimeter and area of irregular shapes by sums of increasingly accurate covering measurements, such as line segments and grids

AC9M8M02.minimum_width: Calculate the volume of a rectangular prism and convert the result between cm³, mL and L.
AC9M8M02.typical_width: Apply volume and capacity to practical problems including optimal packaging, production, and dimension-finding; select appropriate units; convert fluently between cm³, mL, L and m³.
wider: Investigate optimal packaging: for a fixed volume, explore what dimensions minimise surface area for rectangular prisms.
Apply volume and capacity to a production context: given a required capacity and one fixed dimension, find the remaining dimensions.
Explore the relationship between volume units and capacity: demonstrate using 1000 unit cubes = 1 litre in a physical or digital model.
elaborations: using models to demonstrate the number of cubic centimetres in a cubic metre and relating this to capacities of millilitres and litres
solving practical problems involving volume and capacity; for example, optimal packaging and production
choosing which measurements are useful to consider when solving practical problems in context
investigating, reasoning and finding solutions to measurement problems involving dimensions, rates, volume and capacity of objects

AC9M8M03.minimum_width: Calculate the area of a circle given radius; find the radius given area; apply C = 2πr to one practical problem.
AC9M8M03.typical_width: Apply A = πr² and C = 2πr to find any unknown (r, d, C, or A); solve composite shape problems including semicircles and sectors; apply to practical contexts with appropriate units.
wider: Explore traditional weaving designs by First Nations Australians and investigate the significance and use of circles — calculate relevant areas and circumferences in context.
Investigate composite shapes combining circles with other polygons: stadia, athletic tracks, circular windows in rectangular frames.
Explore the connection A = ½ × C × r — explain this geometrically using the sector rearrangement method.
elaborations: deducing that the area of a circle is between 2 radius squares and 4 radius squares, using 3 × radius² as a rough estimate
investigating the area of circles using a square grid or by rearranging a circle divided into smaller and smaller sectors to resemble a close approximation of a rectangle
applying the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle to solve practical problems
exploring traditional weaving designs by First Nations Australians and investigating the significance and use of circles

AC9M8M04.minimum_width: Convert a given time between two time zones using UTC offsets; handle day changes correctly.
AC9M8M04.typical_width: Convert between multiple time zones; apply 12- and 24-hour conventions; solve scheduling and itinerary problems across at least two time zones including daylight saving considerations.
wider: Plan an international travel itinerary across at least three time zones in Asia — calculate all local arrival and departure times.
Investigate the practical challenge of scheduling regular virtual meetings for a company with staff across Australian states and an international office.
Explore why the International Date Line creates calendar day differences and how travellers account for this.
elaborations: using digital tools to investigate time zones around the world and convert from one zone to another, such as time in Perth compared to eastern states
recognising the challenges of planning regular virtual meeting times for a company that has both international staff and staff within different states of Australia
planning an international travel itinerary that covers destinations in different time zones across Asia

AC9M8M05.minimum_width: Identify and write a rate from a practical context; apply a given rate to solve a practical problem.
AC9M8M05.typical_width: Recognise rates in varied real-world contexts (pay rates, cost per unit, recipe ratios, simple interest, average rates); apply rates to unit conversion and practical problem-solving including taxation and currency conversion.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' land management practices involving rates — e.g. rate of fire spread under different environmental conditions.
Use taxation rate tables to calculate annual income tax — compare marginal and effective rates.
Apply currency conversion as a rate problem: plan a budget for overseas travel using current exchange rates.
elaborations: identifying examples of rates in the real world, including constant rates, rate of pay, cost per kilogram, recipes, simple interest and average rates
applying rates to solve problems involving the conversion between different units of measure
applying rates to calculate solutions to problems in different contexts; for example, required run rates in cricket, dilution of concentrated chemicals
using taxation tables to calculate an individual's annual income tax
investigating the application of rates in First Nations Australians' land management practices, including the rate of fire spread under different environmental conditions

AC9M8M06.minimum_width: State Pythagoras' theorem; find the hypotenuse and find a shorter side for given right-angled triangles; verify for a 3-4-5 triangle.
AC9M8M06.typical_width: Apply Pythagoras' theorem to varied practical and geometric problems; classify triangles using side lengths; apply to distance between two points on the Cartesian plane; identify Pythagorean triples.
wider: Investigate different proofs and demonstrations of Pythagoras' theorem from multiple cultures: Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China, Greece — compare approaches.
Apply the theorem to 3D problems: find the diagonal of a rectangular prism using the theorem twice.
Investigate how Pythagoras' theorem determines distance between two points on a Cartesian plane — connect to applications in mapping and predictive text.
elaborations: discussing and comparing different applications, demonstrations and proofs of Pythagoras' theorem, from Egypt and Mesopotamia, Greece, India and China
using Pythagoras' theorem to determine unknown lengths of sides in right-angled triangles and finding lengths in practical problems
recognising the relationship between the squares of lengths of sides for different types of triangles: right-angled, acute or obtuse
identifying Pythagorean triples, such as (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25) and (8,15,17)
investigating how Pythagoras' theorem can be applied to determine the distance between two points in the plane

AC9M8M07.minimum_width: Formulate and solve a practical problem using a ratio or rate model; state which model is appropriate and justify; interpret the solution in context.
AC9M8M07.typical_width: Apply modelling to scales and plans, chemical mixing, currency conversion, income tax, and radiocarbon dating; justify model choice; review model appropriateness; communicate solutions.
wider: Investigate radiocarbon dating as a ratio application — model the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 isotopes to estimate the age of organic material.
Model the ratio applications in First Nations Australians' string and cordage making — investigate the ratio of fibre lengths and twisting rates involved.
Compare simple and refined models for the same situation (e.g. constant vs variable exchange rate) and evaluate which is more appropriate in different circumstances.
elaborations: modelling and solving problems related to situations such as scales on maps and plans, the mixing of chemicals or ingredients, or calculating magnification
modelling problems involving converting money amounts using different exchange rates and applying them when planning and budgeting for overseas travel
modelling situations involving financial contexts; for example, income tax, using taxation rates on annual income
modelling situations involving the use of ratios in radiocarbon dating methods, including the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 isotopes in organic material
modelling situations involving ratio and its application in the making of string and cordage by First Nations Australians

AC9M8P01.minimum_width: Identify the complement of a given event; use P(A) + P(not A) = 1 to find an unknown probability in a practical context.
AC9M8P01.typical_width: Apply the complementary relationship across varied practical contexts; recognise when finding the complement is the more efficient strategy; apply to simple 'at least one' problems.
wider: Investigate how AI applications use complementary event probabilities for binary classification — e.g. spam vs not spam, fraud vs not fraud.
Explore P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) for simple cases — apply to problems where direct calculation requires listing many outcomes.
Investigate contexts where two events are both complementary and mutually exclusive — discuss what this implies about the sample space.
elaborations: understanding that knowing the probability of an event allows the probability of its complement to be found
using the relationship that for a single event A, P(A) + P(not A) = 1
using the sum of probabilities to solve problems, such as the probability of starting a game by throwing a 5 or 6 on a dice
investigating how various applications of artificial intelligence use the probability of complementary events when assessing the likelihood of favourable outcomes

AC9M8P02.minimum_width: Represent all combinations for two events using one method (two-way table, tree diagram, or Venn diagram); calculate P(A and B) and P(A or B).
AC9M8P02.typical_width: Represent two-event combinations using all three methods; calculate probabilities using and, or (inclusive/exclusive), and at least language; distinguish mutually exclusive events; apply to practical situations.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games — e.g. Battendi from the Ngarrindjeri Peoples of Lake Murray — represent combinations and discuss fairness.
Investigate the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) informally — verify using a two-way table.
Apply compound probability to real survey data: the probability a randomly selected student studies both maths and music, or either subject.
elaborations: describing events using language of 'at least', exclusive 'or', inclusive 'or' and 'and'
using Venn diagrams or two-way tables to demonstrate the difference between mutually exclusive events and non-mutually exclusive events
exploring First Nations Australian children's instructive games; for example, Battendi from the Ngarrindjeri Peoples of Lake Murray and Lake Albert

AC9M8P03.minimum_width: Use a digital tool to simulate a compound event for at least 100 trials; record results and compare observed relative frequency to theoretical probability.
AC9M8P03.typical_width: Simulate compound events using multiple digital tools; record outcomes systematically; compare observed relative frequencies to theoretical probabilities; describe results including whether events appear complementary.
wider: Use generative AI to construct and run probability simulations — describe what the tool does and critically evaluate whether its outputs are trustworthy.
Investigate whether long-run simulations confirm that two events are complementary — use as an empirical check on theoretical calculations.
Explore how the number of trials affects convergence to theoretical probability — connect to the law of large numbers from AC9M7P02.
elaborations: using digital tools, including generative artificial intelligence, to conduct probability simulations involving compound events
using a random number generator and digital tools, including generative artificial intelligence, to simulate rolling 2 dice and calculating the difference
using online simulation software to conduct probability simulations to determine in the long run if events are complementary

AC9M8SP01.minimum_width: State the four triangle congruence conditions and identify which applies to a given pair; state the AA similarity condition and use it to find a missing side.
AC9M8SP01.typical_width: Apply all congruence (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) and similarity (AA, SAS, SSS) conditions; calculate scale factors; apply congruence and similarity to other shapes formed by transformations; explain why SSA is not a valid congruence condition.
wider: Apply indirect measurement using similar triangles: measure the height of a building or tree using shadow lengths.
Apply similarity to map scale problems — connect mathematical similarity to ratio modelling from AC9M8M07.
Investigate: is every square similar to every other square? Is every rectangle? Justify using the conditions.
elaborations: developing an understanding of what it means for shapes to be congruent or similar
using the enlargement transformation and digital tools to develop sets of similar shapes
investigating sufficient conditions to establish that 2 triangles are congruent
applying logical reasoning and tests for congruence and similarity to problems and proofs involving plane shapes
comparing angle and side measurements of shapes under transformation to answer questions such as 'What changes?' and 'What stays the same?'
establishing that 2 shapes are congruent if one lies exactly on top of the other after one or more transformations

AC9M8SP02.minimum_width: Use congruent triangles to establish one property of a quadrilateral (e.g. diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other); find an unknown angle using an established property.
AC9M8SP02.typical_width: Establish properties of squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, trapeziums and kites using congruent triangles and angle properties; solve multi-step problems with full geometric reasoning.
wider: Apply quadrilateral properties to construction designs: car jacks, scissor lifts, folding umbrellas — identify which property makes the design functional.
Establish properties of a kite using congruent triangles — prove which diagonal is the axis of symmetry.
Design a multi-step angle problem using quadrilateral properties — write the full solution with reasons.
elaborations: establishing the properties of squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, trapeziums and kites using geometric properties and proof
identifying properties of quadrilaterals related to side lengths, parallel sides, angles, diagonals and symmetry
applying the properties of triangles and quadrilaterals to construction designs such as car jacks, scissor lifts, folding umbrellas, toolboxes

AC9M8SP03.minimum_width: Plot and read coordinates (x, y, z) in the first octant; describe the position of an object using latitude, longitude and altitude.
AC9M8SP03.typical_width: Describe positions in 3D using coordinate systems and real-world reference systems; compare 2D and 3D coordinate systems; use dynamic geometry software to construct shapes in 3D.
wider: Investigate how 3D printers use a three-dimensional coordinate system to build objects layer by layer — describe the relationship between coordinate path and physical object.
Explore geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australian communities to describe position and transformation on Country.
Interpret 3D coordinate locations for objects in multi-storey car parks or games — connect abstract coordinates to physical navigation.
elaborations: locating aircraft/drones using latitude, longitude and altitude as a three-dimensional coordinate system
constructing three-dimensional objects using 3D printers or designing software that uses a three-dimensional coordinate system
comparing and contrasting two-dimensional and three-dimensional coordinate systems
using dynamic geometry software to construct shapes and objects within the first octant of a three-dimensional coordinate system
interpreting three-dimensional coordinate locations for objects in multi-storey car parks; playing games based on three-dimensional coordinate systems
exploring position and transformation through geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australians' communities

AC9M8SP04.minimum_width: Design a flowchart that correctly classifies triangles as congruent or not using at least two congruence conditions; trace a given algorithm with two test inputs.
AC9M8SP04.typical_width: Design and test algorithms for congruence and similarity classification covering all conditions; trace and evaluate given algorithms for correctness; describe how the algorithm works in plain language.
wider: Extend the algorithm to classify quadrilaterals as congruent or similar — identify what additional conditions are needed.
Implement a classification algorithm in a simple programming language — test with generated sets of triangle measurements.
Investigate the minimum number of decision steps needed to distinguish all outcomes (congruent by SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS; similar; neither).
elaborations: listing the properties or criteria necessary to determine if shapes are similar or congruent
using the conditions for congruence of triangles and similarity of triangles to develop a sorting algorithm; for example, creating a flow chart
evaluating algorithms for accuracy in classifying and distinguishing between similar and congruent triangles

AC9M8ST01.minimum_width: Distinguish census from sampling; identify an appropriate collection technique for a given situation and justify the choice; identify one source of bias in a described data collection process.
AC9M8ST01.typical_width: Compare census, sampling, experiment and observation as techniques; evaluate practicalities and implications; explain how bias affects conclusions; suggest methods to reduce identified biases.
wider: Investigate how decisions concerning sampling relate to training AI systems — explain why biased training data leads to biased AI outputs.
Explore voluntary response bias in online surveys — design a class experiment to demonstrate its effect.
Investigate a real case of biased data collection and its consequences — connect to ethical implications of data misuse.
elaborations: identifying situations where data can be collected by census and those where a sample is appropriate
investigating the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through sampling, using a variety of investigative processes
discussing how observations, experiments and sampling methods can be impacted by bias
using digital tools such as simulations and digital measuring devices to observe, measure and record data
investigating how decisions concerning sampling relate to the training of artificial intelligence systems, recognising the need to mitigate any potential bias

AC9M8ST02.minimum_width: Describe simple random and systematic sampling; collect a sample using a specified method; display the distribution and report key features.
AC9M8ST02.typical_width: Compare simple random, systematic, stratified, quota and convenience sampling for reliability and bias; analyse distributions from primary and secondary sources; report on shape, centre and spread with commentary on sampling method.
wider: Investigate primary and secondary data sources relating to reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians — analyse sampling methods and evaluate representativeness.
Demonstrate how stratification improves representativeness when a population has distinct subgroups.
Investigate secondary data from ABS or similar sources — evaluate the sampling methodology used and how it affects confidence in findings.
elaborations: investigating different methods of sampling used to collect data, considering the source and size of samples
comparing the sampling methods of simple random, systematic, stratified, quota, clustered or convenience, or judgement, and discussing the reliability of each
defining and distinguishing between probabilistic terms such as random, sample space, sample and sample distribution
investigating primary and secondary data sources relating to reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians

AC9M8ST03.minimum_width: Compare two samples from the same population and explain why the distributions differ; state that larger samples produce less variation.
AC9M8ST03.typical_width: Use digital simulation to compare distributions from multiple samples; describe variation in means, medians and proportions; demonstrate that increasing sample size reduces variation; apply to prediction contexts.
wider: Investigate First Nations Ranger Groups' use of sampling to track biodiversity — explain why sampling variation affects conservation conclusions.
Explore how AI and machine learning systems require large training datasets to reduce model performance variation — connect to the statistical principle.
Investigate the effect of adding or removing outliers on measures of central tendency and spread across different sample sizes.
elaborations: comparing the proportion of students in favour of a proposal between different random samples of 50 students from the same school
using digital tools to simulate repeated sampling of the same population, recording and comparing means, medians and proportions
using relative frequencies from historical data to predict proportions and the likely number of outcomes in situations such as weather forecasting
investigating the effect that adding or removing data from a data set has on measures of central tendency and spread
investigating First Nations Ranger Groups and other groups' use of sampling techniques to track biodiversity of species
exploring how the comparison of variations in distributions from the same population applies to data-driven decision-making

AC9M8ST04.minimum_width: Plan a statistical investigation specifying the population, sampling method, and ethical consideration; collect a sample; make one inference and acknowledge one source of uncertainty.
AC9M8ST04.typical_width: Plan and conduct investigations using ethical and fair sampling methods; analyse distributions; make inferences about the population; report findings with explicit acknowledgement of uncertainty and connection to sample size.
wider: Investigate progress in reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians — evaluate ethical considerations in sampling and reporting for sensitive social topics.
Compare inferences drawn from two different sample sizes for the same population — discuss how sample size changes confidence.
Explore how statistical uncertainty is communicated in public health or environmental reporting — compare with how uncertainty is often omitted in media.
elaborations: using data such as electricity consumption to draw conclusions about the impacts of events, such as pandemics, on households or businesses
identifying situations where the collection of data from a sample is necessary due to efficiency, cost or restricted time
exploring progress in reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians, investigating and evaluating sampling techniques
